To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the expert performance framework (Ericsson, 2006) is an appropriate framework for the study of reproducibly superior achievement; (b) the expert performance research has provided a large body of evidence supporting the expert performance framework, which is summarized in a general model; and (c) the evidence from the expert performance research does not support the existence of innate talents, with the exception of genetic factors determining body height.

(1) there is no evidence that any human being is so genetically endowed that he or she is destined to be superior in any particular domain of achievement, (2) there are many domains of exceptional performance in which the best performers are clearly superior to the average performers, (3) in these domains, the best performers have engaged in extended periods of deliberate effort, and (4) the superior performance of the best performers can be attributed to the physiological adaptations and complex mechanisms that emerge from this deliberate

1) superior reproducible performance in any domain is acquired by extensive deliberate practice; 2) the acquisition of superior performance requires the development of a complex cognitive mechanism; and 3) superior performance in any domain requires a physiological basis for the cognitive mechanism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theoretical framework for the identification of evidence for reproducible superior performance.
identifying the conditions under which individuals attain superior performance, and how they do it.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
giftedness is the potential for superior reproducible achievement, and that this potential is not innate but rather the product of a complex interaction between genetic endowment and environment.
there is no scientific evidence for innate talents, but there is abundant evidence for reproducibility of superior performance in a wide range of domains.
there is no evidence for innate constraints on the attainment of exceptional performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the evidence for reproducible performance is not consistent with the idea of innate talent, but rather that the attainment of exceptional performance is the product of complex interactions of genetic factors, physiological adaptations and cognitive mechanisms, all of which are shaped and constrained by environmental factors.

the evidence for innate talent is limited to the genetic factors that determine body height, and that the evidence for the existence of innate talents in other domains is limited to the existence of genes that predispose individuals to develop a talent.
the evidence for innate constraints is very weak and the evidence for superior performance emerging from extended periods of deliberate training is very strong.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the expert performance framework can provide a general framework for the study of giftedness, and that there is no evidence to support a claim that giftedness can be defined as an innate talent that is not dependent on the attainment of high levels of achievement.

the concept of giftedness is not supported by evidence for superior innate ability, but is rather an emergent property of extended periods of deliberate, domain specific practice that result in superior performance.
there is no evidence that supports the idea that giftedness is a separate category from high levels of achievement.
